one_liner: Static C++17 k-d tree that indexes boxes as well as points; out-queries Boost.Geometry's R*-tree on bulk-loaded data.
what_it_does: KdBoxTree is a read-only, in-memory spatial index over points or axis-aligned boxes in any dimension and scalar type. You construct it from a std::vector of elements (it takes ownership), then run range (box-window) queries through a visitor callback, an index-returning overload or an iterator, and k-nearest queries. Its interface differs from boost::geometry::index::rtree: there are no predicates/query adaptors and no insert or remove, and any change means rebuilding with Create(). It ships inside GeoToolbox, a spatial-index benchmark harness that also drives Boost R*-tree, nanoflann, GEOS STR-tree and tidwall's R-tree.
how_it_is_fast: It is a k-d tree built top-down by midpoint splits on the longest axis of each node's bounding box, with in-place partitioning of a flat element array and nodes kept in one contiguous vector (leaf size 32 by default). Boxes that straddle a split plane go into a third 'middle' child, which is then split only on the other axes, so a box index keeps cheap k-d descent instead of the overlapping MBRs an R-tree has. Each node stores the tight bound of its elements, so a query can return a whole subtree without per-element tests once the window contains the node. An optional StoreSpatialKeys template flag keeps a contiguous copy of the keys so scans need no pointer chasing (about 1.2x faster at the largest sizes, for more memory).
when_to_use: Bulk-loaded static point or box sets (10^3 to 10^6 elements) queried many times: the README measures it as the fastest index to bulk-load and pays back its build cost within about 100 queries versus a linear scan
Range/window queries on 2D or 3D box keys (GIS footprints, parcels, mesh triangle bounds), where it ranks first on average ahead of Boost R*-tree, GEOS and tidwall
k-nearest queries on box keys: Boost R*-tree is the only other index in the comparison that supports them, and KdBoxTree is faster
Point range queries from 10^4 elements upward, or point kNN at 10^6 elements and on strongly structured data, where it passes nanoflann
Code that needs float or double keys, more than 2 dimensions, and a custom allocator (the template takes a TElementAllocator)
when_not_to_use: Data that changes: there is no insert or erase. Use Boost R*-tree or tidwall rtree.c for dynamic sets
Point kNN below about 10^5 elements, or a minimal memory footprint: nanoflann wins both
2D box range queries on Polygon-like (ring-shaped) data, where GEOS STR-tree is faster, or 2D boxes around 10^4-10^5 elements, where tidwall is
Fewer than about 100 queries on about 100 elements: the README says an index tops out at 1.2-2x over a plain std::vector scan at that size
Production use where maturity matters: 0 stars, no releases or tags, a single author, and the README says it is tested only on Windows

integration.dependencies: none for the index itself: KdBoxTree.hpp plus GeoToolbox's own GeometryTools/Span/SpatialTools headers and the standard library. Eigen is optional; Catch2, Shapelib and LodePNG are only for the tests and benchmarks
integration.min_toolchain: C++17; tested with MSVC 2026 and Clang 22 on Windows
integration.platforms: Tested only on Windows x64 (README). The core code is plain portable C++, but the repo's CMake adds /arch:AVX2 (MSVC) or -msse4.2 (other compilers), so on non-x86 targets you build the header yourself
integration.thread_safety: not documented (queries are const member functions over immutable storage, so concurrent reads look safe, but the author does not state it)
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial: it replaces the bulk-loaded (packing constructor) use of boost::geometry::index::rtree for intersects-window and k-nearest queries, but the API is different and there is no insert/remove, no predicate composition and no Boost.Geometry type adaptation

gotchas: IndexType is int, so one tree holds fewer than 2^31 elements

The constructor takes the element vector by value and reorders it during the build. Queries hand back elements by reference or as indices into the tree's own reordered copy, not into your original vector
StoreSpatialKeys defaults to false, but the published benchmark results were measured with it on. Turning it on raises memory on box keys slightly above Boost R*-tree
Splits are at the box midpoint, not the median. Coincident points or rounding make a split fail, which leaves that node an oversized leaf; heavily duplicated keys can therefore produce large leaves
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick it over nanoflann when the keys are boxes, or when you have points at 10^6 scale or need range queries above 10^4 elements. Pick it over tidwall rtree.c when the data is static and large or unevenly spread and you need kNN or runtime-chosen dimensions/scalar types. tidwall, and Boost R*-tree for its versatility, remain the choice for dynamic data, and TG is for polygon predicates rather than indexing.
verified_claims_summary: The author's own harness compares KdBoxTree with Boost.Geometry 1.90 R*-tree, nanoflann 1.10.1, GEOS 3.14.1 STR-tree and tidwall rtree.c on synthetic and real 2D/3D point and box sets of 10^2-10^6 elements. It was built with MSVC 2026 and Clang 22 on an ASUS ROG Strix G16 laptop under Windows 11 (CPU model not stated; the repo's CMake sets /arch:AVX2 plus /GL /LTCG on MSVC and -msse4.2 -flto on Clang). The README reports rankings, not a KdBoxTree-vs-Boost ratio: KdBoxTree builds fastest and wins range queries and box kNN, and Boost 'lags behind in query performance'; raw TSVs are in ikolev21/ikolev21.github.io.
status_note: Active single-author project (last commit 2026-09-06, no releases, 0 stars) under BSL-1.0; the index is one roughly 1,300-line header plus a few helper headers, so vendoring it is straightforward.
